extracted.intended_audience: novelists, fiction writers, and students of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on managing narrator, point of view, and the balance between pictorial narration and dramatic enactment in novels; when to use first-person, how to authenticate a narrator, and how to economize dramatic scenes. Uses examples from Thackeray, Flaubert, Maupassant, Dickens, Meredith, Turgenev, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture vs Drama (pictorial method vs dramatic enactment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between the 'picture' (a reflected, panoramic view that represents the author’s mind) and 'drama' (enactment, a scene presented as though caught in the act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The picture passes into a book as a review of many details and occasions; drama places us close to the facts and makes the scene seem contemporaneous and self-telling. Examples: Maupassant's work is closer to drama; Thackeray's to picture. Use drama for intensity and climax; rely on pictorial narration for breadth, but be aware each method's strengths and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conspicuous omniscient author
rubrics_metrics.description: When much of a novel is pictorial/narrative rather than dramatic, the omniscient author is apt to become conspicuous and questionably authoritative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conspicuous narrator can leave the book feeling 'not complete in itself' or 'not really self-contained'. Prudent novelists should avoid unnecessarily straining the convention of omniscience; if the narrator is noticeable in a way the book cannot justify, the general impression can feel thin or ineffectual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize the narrator's point of view (authenticate the seeing eye)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the mind and eye that know the story objective by including or dramatizing the point of view within the book so it can be recognized and verified there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the narrator's viewpoint is presented as a fact in the story (a demonstrable perspective or a character's vision), it silences questioning about narrator authority and makes every side of the book equally finished. Examples: Thackeray later includes the narrator in-character (Esmond) to pack the 'loose end' into the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of first-person 'characterized I' to give precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace the loose, general authorial 'I' with a characterized first-person narrator—an 'I' who is a known, named participant in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The characterized 'I' gives a definite field of vision and a personal tone that becomes part of the story, lending precision and individuality. Good for long retrospects or when a consistent vantage point is needed (examples: Esmond, David Copperfield). Beware loss of freedom and other snares when the narrator must also serve larger dramatic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economize dramatic enactment (hoard drama)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat drama as the novelist’s 'highest light' and avoid using it prodigally where it is not needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using dramatic scenes too often lessens their force; the economical procedure is to reserve dramatic enactment for important occasions (e.g., climaxes, moments requiring intensity), thus preserving their impact. Bovary is quoted as an example where drama is used sparingly and effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and manage scene vs narration
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist’s quality appears in how he guides the story into scenes and extracts it from scenes—how he manages the interplay of pictorial narration and dramatic enactment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novels often need both: narration for breadth and travel of experience, drama for intensity. The writer should decide when to convert narration into scene (for emphasis) and when to summarize (for scope). Overuse of scenes in everyday novels both neglects scene treatment and wastes its value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make recollection/action visible (dramatize memory)
rubrics_metrics.description: When narrating past events, treat the recollecting mind as an active element—'a piece of action'—and dramatize recollection so that the relation between recorder and remembered events is part of the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rendering memory itself as action (a play-within-a-play) authenticates the account and gives it double duty: it both authenticates the picture and provides independent interest. This helps close the gap between authorial knowledge and what the reader can test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first-person to unify sprawling or episodic narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: A first-person narrator can supply an organic unity to rambling, fragmentary, or retrospective narratives simply by belonging to all parts of the tale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Autobiographical form composes 'of its own accord' because the hero’s act of telling links disparate episodes. Examples: David Copperfield and Harry Richmond—first-person helps draw together long stretches of past experience. But beware that apparent formlessness may mask other structural needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure narrator's reports are testable by the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid letting authorial commentary or supplied information rest solely on the narrator's unsupported assertion; readers give less weight to facts they cannot verify through the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turgenev's habit of drawing the reader aside to 'pour information' exemplifies this anti-pattern: such information 'will never have its due weight' because it is untestable. Prefer dramatized evidence or inclusion of the narrator within the scene so the reader can judge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make point-of-view inclusion finish the book's design
rubrics_metrics.description: If the narrator’s relation to the story is left unaccounted, the book may have 'a loose end'—include the point of view within the book to produce an integral design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A book torn away from its author must 'bring its own recognisances'; including or dramatizing the viewpoint prevents an inconclusive look that draws the eye away from the book itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select narrator mode to suit the book’s subject (narrator as subject vs reporter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose whether the narrator is the central subject of the book (as in a portrait of a man) or primarily a reporter of an expanse of life (as in Dickens's Copperfield).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the book’s aim is to portray the narrator's moral and emotional history (Meredith’s Harry Richmond), the first-person narrator must be treated as protagonist and scenes must enact his development. If the aim is to show the spectacle of many characters (Copperfield), the narrator may be primarily a collecting eye.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial scenes must have dramatic function when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: When the story’s subject is the narrator or when a character’s development is the book’s aim, pictorial episodes must contribute actively to that character’s enactment and change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Harry Richmond, the episodes are not mere pictures but serve to enact and effect Harry’s transformation; pictorial material should 'do something as well as be' when the narrative requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid casual or careless use of narrator-in-character devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Including the narrator as a character can solve the problem of authorial conspicuousness, but must be handled with care; careless use can be clumsy or inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thackeray's use of the narrator 'in character' is described as loose and casual at times; although it helps 'pick up the loose end', overuse without proper care can be awkward. Use dramatization of the narrator thoughtfully and consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use narration to cover wide ranges, drama for concentrated intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration (pictorial method) enables a novelist to cover great spaces of life and quantities of experience; drama supplies intensity and is appropriate where impressions must be emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As plots thicken and climaxes approach, narration should give place to enactment. The novelist must accept that breadth often needs narration but should 'make good' the loss of intensity by dramatizing where possible.
